title: The quail and the creeper
hookLine: a quail held by a rotten creeper, an elephant held by a thick rope: it depends what you believe binds you

lines: A QUAIL IN A ROTTEN VINE.
cards: A little brown quail is caught in a tangle of rotten vine. One good tug and the vine would snap. But the quail doesn't tug.

It sits there, trapped, until the hunter comes. Now picture a royal elephant, a full-grown tusker, tied with thick leather straps. It shrugs its shoulders, the straps break, and it walks off wherever it likes.
Which one is really bound? The sixty-sixth sutta says: that depends less on the rope than you'd think.

teach.b: It starts with a monk named Udāyin, alone, feeling grateful. The Buddha, he remembers, asked the monks to give up eating in the afternoon, and later at night. Some grumbled: must we give up even this little thing?
Then Udāyin remembers why it mattered. Monks walking for alms in the pitch dark had stumbled into cesspits and thornbushes.
Once, he says, a woman washing a pot saw him by a flash of lightning and screamed that a demon was after her. He's glad now. The Buddha answers with the quail.
Some people, told to give up some small thing, say: what, this trifle? And they resent it. For them, that small thing is a strong, thick, tough bond, the way the rotten creeper is for the quail.
Others give up the small thing easily, and for them even a thick rope is weak. Then he brings it home.

teach.h: THE POOR HUT, THE RICH HOUSE.
teach.b: A poor man with a leaking hut, a single bad bed, a pot of rice, can't bring himself to give any of it up. A rich householder with stores of gold might walk away from all of it. The size of the thing isn't the point.

teach.h: WHAT BINDS IS THE HOLDING ON.
teach.b: What binds is the holding on. It's everywhere: the one more episode at midnight, the phone you check without wanting to, the argument you can't drop though you've forgotten what it's about. Each one is a rotten creeper.
It looks like a rope because nobody has pulled. And the sutta is honest: the creeper doesn't snap by itself. Somebody has to pull.
The good news is it's only a creeper.

how: Buddhist monastics give up eating after midday, and teachers use this sutta to show students that small renunciations are often the hardest, and that letting go of a little thing can loosen a whole habit.

o: a quail, held by a vine it could snap
a royal elephant that breaks its straps
a hunter who sets traps in the vines

games.q: who's bound by what: tap the pairs.
p: grateful for giving up night meals
can't give up his leaking hut

s: the sutta says big possessions bind more tightly than small ones
a poor man may cling to a leaking hut; what binds is the holding on.
Udāyin remembers a woman who saw him by lightning on a night alms round and screamed
she thought a demon was after her; it's one reason he's glad the night meal was given up.
the creeper in the story is strong and tough
it's rotten. it only holds because the quail never pulls.

games.q: you're asked to give up something tiny, a late-night habit. what does the sutta say makes it hard?
o: how much you hold on to it
how strict the person asking is
games.why: for one who resents giving it up, even a trifle is a thick bond; for one who lets go, even a thick rope is weak.

practice: Let one small habit come to mind, something you keep doing that you'd rather not, a snack, a scroll, a sharp reply, and picture it as a thin, dry vine wrapped around you. Feel how much it seems to hold.
Then, on an out-breath, picture yourself simply standing up, and the vine snapping, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Latukika. The quail: a rotten vine holds it only because it never pulls, while thick straps can't hold the elephant.

orig.note: Pali laṭukikā: the quail. the sutta is named for it, the Laṭukikopama, 'the simile of the quail'.

carryVoice: Your line: it's only a creeper. What binds is the holding on. Day four hundred fifty-eight, done.
